### **Crossing The Street**
Saturday morning found me in the standard conditions of the American political writer: under-caffeinated, over-curious, and operating on substantially less sleep than any responsible human should allow himself to function on. Sleep was no longer a partner; sleep was a creditor.
I finished the farm chores, grabbed the camera, and headed for Castor HQ, with one stop at the local coffee house for a cup of black brew strong enough to restart whatever was left of the nervous system.
Weeks earlier I'd taken the temperature of my own party, from parking lots, sidewalks, and half-empty halls across Republican America. The rebel waves. The factions sniffing at the vacuum that opens the day Trump's term ends. That was the easy gig. This morning, I was crossing the street.
During my own run for Congress, I'd gotten to know Neil Manimala, a Democratic candidate for Hillsborough County Commission, a decent man knocking doors in the heat for an office most people can't name. I asked to tag along one Saturday, to look the Democrat voter in the eye outside the ballrooms and the press conferences. He invited me to a joint door-knocking event with Congressman Kathy Castor.
Kathy Castor. The champion with the belt.
A powerhouse for over a decade, now in the fight of her life, not because of the challenger, but because of the arena. Somebody redrew the map and moved the ring while she was still standing in it. Home-field advantage, gone. I'd watched her from the nosebleeds. I'd reviewed the tape. I'd imagined the debate stage over and over again.
And now here she was, ten feet away, working the room like a woman who had personally requested every one of these people's Saturday mornings. Hugs and handshakes freely going around. This was no laptop campaign run out of a basement to a mailing list. This was the ancient and thoroughly undignified business of asking human beings for help with your face.
I was impressed, and I hated being impressed.
The room held maybe thirty people, every age, every color. Signs on every flat surface, signs stacked against the walls, signs leaning on signs like drunks propping up drunks. No chairs. Thirty volunteers and not one chair. A set designer had built a movie set of a campaign and forgotten the furniture. A real campaign headquarters. And a movie set. Both. That's the whole country in one room, if you squint.
Since the threshold, a low electric dread had been building in my sternum**.** Not a country-club Republican who writes a check and goes home, the actual guy who'd tried to take her belt. Would they smell it on me? Would some sharp-eyed volunteer with a clipboard call me out in front of thirty strangers? Or worse, would they just assume I was one of them and start telling me secrets I wasn't supposed to hear?
Kathy made her rounds, shaking hands, thanking people, making each of them feel like the most important person in Hillsborough County. When she got to me, she put out her hand.
"Thank you for coming, it's good to see you."
"Kathy, it's good to finally meet you. I'm Gavriel."
Something flickered behind her eyes, perhaps recognition, perhaps a recollection she couldn't quite pin down. Then she moved along to the man on my left. Which meant she knew, or she didn't, and I couldn't tell, and not knowing wasn't any better.
Then Castor called the room to silence. She talked about the week's goal, veterans, about respect for the military, about the work she'd keep doing in Congress.
"Why don't we all introduce ourselves--"
And here it came again, the question I'd been carrying since the parking lot. Announce I'm here for The American Kitchen Table, writing about the state of their party, and lose the chance to see, unadulterated, what drags a person off the couch to knock on strangers' doors?
"--and if you have a rank or a title, introduce yourself with that."
She handed me a clean out. Thank G-d.
The veterans went first. A man stood and introduced himself as the first Black general in Special Forces, General Remo Butler. Two others who were retired colonels, one of them West Point. Then my turn.
I stood up and said the truth, albeit not the whole truth.
"I'm PFC Soriano, invited by Neil. I served in the US Army; the military is my family's legacy. My wife served too. First the Army, then the Navy. So, as you can imagine, it got interesting around the house during the Army-Navy games. Go Army!"
Everyone laughed.
I thought, Beautiful, I've survived. I could go back to being furniture, a quiet man near the signs, watching the machine work.
### **Good Morning, America**
Retired Gen. Remo took charge the way I imagine he took charge of everything for thirty years, and nobody in the room was dumb enough to tell him no, so he set the room himself. He started praising Kathy's work for veterans, then he told us all we needed to come together and carry her across the finish line. It was a moving speech. I sat there wondering how many versions of that speech he'd given in his life, in how many rooms, to how many men who needed to hear it.
Then he called it. "Let's get a photo. All of us vets."
I pressed myself deeper into the wall. The old trick. The one you learn when you'd rather be furniture, the one that works right up until it doesn't. Today it didn't. My age and my face and whatever else they saw in me made sure I stuck out like a thumb.
Neil and I traded a look. I couldn't read his. I don't know what mine said, but I'd bet it said please, G-d, not today.
I mumbled something about humbly declining. They insisted. And here's the thing, you don't deny fellow men in arms a photo. Doesn't matter what banner you fly, what ballot you pull, who you voted for last time. You both put on that uniform. That's a debt that doesn't care about party. I reluctantly unpeeled myself from the wall and got in the frame.
A general. Two colonels. A PFC who'd spent the last ten minutes trying to merge through drywall.
The commotion of everybody fighting for a spot in the frame. One of the colonels, a small bent-over old man, kept shuffling around hunting for an angle he liked, like a man trying to find the good side of a bad hand.
I was second from the General. Shoulder to shoulder. Photo face on.
Then he started talking.
Everyone stared at us. And that's when it landed on me like an almighty clean right hand from Iron Mike that knocked out Michael Spinks in 91 seconds: this was not a photo. This was an endorsement video. Remo was speaking, live, red dot burning, and I was standing in the shot.
"Good morning. I'm Brigadier General, retired, Special Forces, Remo Butler. I am supporting Congresswoman Kathy Castor for reelection because she shows what it's all about. She reaches across the aisle. She knows how to talk to everyone. And she will work very, very hard for us, and she will make this an inclusive party."
My head was spinning like I'd slammed five shots of whiskey back-to-back on an empty stomach. The general finished. Then he looked at me. Just a look. And somewhere in the back of my skull a single word detonated:
## **#@!**
I could see everything happening to me and through me at the same time, like watching my own body get hijacked from the cheap seats. Every exit ran through the same two problems: don't embarrass Neil, and don't be the one**** who ruins the momentum the room just built. Two simple rules and a live microphone pointed at my face.
I said the only thing that showed up to work that morning.
I support her support for veterans.
That's what I remember saying. That's what my mouth did while my brain stood off to the side, hands on hips, watching in horror. And the whole time I was cursing myself. Fanatically. A running filibuster of self-loathing in the privacy of my own skull while my face delivered calm, measured, veteran-adjacent words into a rolling camera.
Here's the funny thing, I've answered hostile questions at candidate forums. I've learned how explosives work as a combat engineer, how to read a fuse, how to time a charge, how to stay calm when the thing in your hands wants to kill you. All of that. All of that was easier than this. Standing shoulder to shoulder with a general and a live red dot, being asked to choose a tribe in real time. A bomb you can study. A camera eats you alive.
The rest followed. More words. I don't fully remember which ones. And when it was over, I was flooded with this pathetic, enormous relief, not because I'd said the right thing, but because it was done. The line had moved. The room had moved on. For one shining second, I was free.
I knew I'd have to deal with this later. But right now? I was just a writer again. Camera around my neck. Nobody looking at me.
For now.
We combat engineers have an unofficial saying. It's our problem until it isn't anymore. Meaning, while you're working the charge, the thing is yours to handle. The second it stops being your problem, it's because you're dead. So, either way, problem solved. Very comforting.
Standing in that frame, live red dot, a general's words rolling through me, and every exit closing at once, I remembered the saying. It was my problem. Unfortunately, I was still alive, which meant I had to keep dealing with it.
### **The Ground Game**
The parking lot was empty. Thirty people had filled that war room thirty-five minutes ago and now gone. Vanished. Like they'd been rented for the hour and returned when the shoot wrapped. I stood in the lot wondering if any of them had actually lived here or if they all materialized for the camera and dissolved back into whatever furniture they came from.
I rode with Josh. Neil's campaign manager. A kid, early twenties, tall, slim, looking exactly like the generation that's supposed to be too busy playing video games at two in the morning to care about anything. Except he did care. He wanted in. Wanted to be part of the change. Same kids the pundits write off, except this one was driving me around Tampa with a clipboard and a plan.
We took off. And then he showed me the app.
This is where I started feeling stupid. You type in the zone numbers, the addresses pop up on a map, you tap one, and it hands you everything: the script, the talking points, instructions for what to do when the door opens and what to do when nobody answers. Door-to-door canvassing, fully automated. Push-button politics. A whole voter file turned into a game you could play with your thumb.
It took me straight back to the days I worked at FedEx. Same system. Same maps, same little address pins, same beeping little machine telling a grown man where to go and what to say when he got there. I'd spent years working that kind of route without ever once thinking of it as political strategy.
And then it hit me, sitting in a kid's car, watching him drive with one hand and point at a screen with the other.
I had run my own congressional campaign barebones. Bare knuckles. No app. No map. No script. Just me, a clipboard, and whatever charm I could scrape together at a stranger's door. Meanwhile the other side had a generation of Josh's running the block like a video game.
The kid wasn't the future of the party. The kid was the party. And I'd been running against it with a pencil.
Once Josh and I left Castor HQ, we got to talking in the car. I was asking him questions, trying to understand what makes a kid his age sign up for this.
He told me he'd always cared about politics, that his generation cared too, they just didn't show up. He was one of the ones who did.
I asked him whether he'd noticed a rebel faction in his own party, people who wanted to vote against anything with the word establishment stamped on it.
When I said the word, he paused. As if he didn't understand the word in this context.
Then he answered. "Yeah, there was a group. A faction that hated corporate candidates. Politicians tied to the corporate machine."
And that's when I started noticing it.
Every time I said establishment, he said corporate.
Same frustration. Same enemy. Different word.
It's the difference between Spanish dialects. A Puerto Rican and a Chilean both speak Spanish but say guagua to one and you're talking about a bus, say it to the other and you're talking about a baby. Same language. Different map. And you can stand there shouting bus, bus, bus at the downtown express and a man turns around frantically looking for a baby.
American politics. Same frustration, different dialect.
We got to the doors. I looked at the itinerary. Castor had told the room herself: non-MAGA Republicans, independents, disillusioned Democrats, Libertarians. Not the base. The middle. Smart, if you're trying to win.
The doors themselves were the real education. I knocked twelve. Spoke to four.
What surprised me wasn't what these people believed. It was how little they'd thought about it at all.
I asked what issues were hurting them. They'd shrug. Cost of living? Yeah. Insurance? Yeah, that too. They agreed with whatever I suggested and offered almost nothing of their own. Not disengaged exactly. Just elsewhere. Living their lives while politics happened around them like weather.
But one voter stuck out to me.
An African American man, mid-thirties, in his garage behind a screen. He was busy cleaning pieces of a machine he'd taken apart, laid out neat on a cloth like a surgeon's tray. The garage was spotless. Couch against the wall. Sports paraphernalia nailed up like trophies. A TV, a cooler, a shelf of odds and ends. A proper man cave. A place a man goes to feel small on purpose, to get away from the world and its troubles and just be nobody for a while.
The kind of man who cared about his country and his community, you could feel it coming off him without him saying a word about it.
And yet. Uninspired. By everyone.
I gave him the spiel. He told me the Republicans had already come by.
"Yeah, they came before. Honestly, I don't know who I'm voting for. I don't even know if I'm going to vote."
"You've got a lot going on," I said. "Last thing you've got time for is sifting through candidates and the bs."
He chuckled. "For sure. I don't know. I really don't know. I know I have to vote, but I don't know."
I asked what he wanted elected officials to fix.
"Honestly? I don't know."
"Cost of living?"
He shrugged. "Yeah, things are more expensive."
He never got up from the chair. Never stopped cleaning the machine. Thanked me and admitted he hadn't looked into the election, said it like a confession, like he was letting me down, like the whole thing was one more chore on a list already too long.
I've sold things for a living, and I know the sound of a door that's still open. He wasn't gone. He wasn't a lost vote. He was a man sitting on the line of certainty, waiting for the right person to make him believe again. Somebody had to show up and give him a reason. Nobody had. Not us Republicans. And not the Democrats.
We parted on good terms. He stayed in the chair. The machine stayed in pieces.
He wasn't excited about anyone.
Neither was anyone else I talked to.
The campaigns come. They knock. They deliver. They leave. But does anyone believe?
### **The Man & The Machine**
After my doors I met up with Josh. He gave me one more address, then we'd be done. On our walk back to the car he told me about a Venezuelan woman he'd been speaking with in Spanish, complaining about Trump and Venezuela, and I wondered how much he understood.
"That's odd, most Venezuelans I speak with are happy about what's going on."
We finally got back to the car and drove off. I kept asking questions. This time about David Jolly.
"Well, there's a reason I'm not out knocking doors for Jolly. I come from a circle of progressive liberals, my friends and I, and Jolly isn't progressive enough. Too much of a reach across."
Then the punchline.
"But I'll vote for him."
And there it was.
The exact same contradiction I'd spent the whole year writing about on my side of the aisle. Voters who hate the establishment, who say the party abandoned them, who won't lift a finger for the candidate, and who show up anyway and pull the lever with their name on it.
I'd written about this among anti-establishment Republicans. Now a progressive Democrat was handing me the same disease.
I was frank with him: "Purely looking at this with the eye of a strategist, Jolly's exactly what you need. You want to win Florida? You need somebody who reaches past the base. Independents. Disillusioned Republicans. The middle. You can't win the governorship by campaigning to the people who already agree with you."
Then we got to the presidential race. Was there anybody progressives wanted?
He didn't have an answer.
"Well, no, not really. Kamala. None of us want Kamala. That's ridiculous. Newsom. We don't want Newsom either. He's corporate. He's such a corporate machine."
Corporate. Again. The word had been tailing us all day like a puppy dog.
Yet when I asked who he felt in his heart should be the nominee? Nothing. He knew who he hated. He didn't know who he loved. He knew the type of politician he was against. Couldn't name the one he was for.
Sound familiar?
I'd heard Republicans say almost the exact same thing about their own leadership. And I didn't leave convinced Josh would sit out a Harris or Newsom nomination, either. He'd vote Jolly despite hating him. That's the tell.
Republicans complain about the establishment. Democrats complain about the corporate machine. Republicans say the party sold out its voters to the establishment. Democrats say it sold out to corporations. Both have a base that feels ignored. Both have a faction that thinks the party betrayed its soul. Both vote the nominee anyway in November.
That doesn't make the parties the same. Different philosophies. Different policies. Different country, maybe. But the feeling? The feeling was the same feeling in a different suit.
By the end of the drive, it had all come together, and the thing that tied it shut was that one word. Corporate. That was Josh's word for establishment. Two rooms, two dialects, one broken machine, and everybody yelling bus, bus, bus at a man who only hears baby.
Republicans scream establishment. Democrats scream corporate. Both mean the same thing: the guys with the money and the microphone rigged it, and nobody's coming to fix your street. Same disease, two dialects, and both sides convinced the other room is full of devils who wouldn't understand a word of it.
I stood in both rooms this year. I watched a loyalist beg eight people to hold a line that had already snapped. I watched a progressive kid who'd hate the governor he was going to vote for anyway. And in between, in a spotless garage, I watched a good man sit still in a chair, cleaning a machine that was already in pieces, because nobody had given him one single reason to believe.
The campaigns will knock again. They'll hand out the same script in a different accent and call it a movement. And the man in the garage will still be sitting there, machine in pieces, waiting for somebody to give him a reason.
**-- Gavriel Soriano**

Different Maps. | | | Oct 14| | | ∙| | Guest post ---|---|--- | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- The "press view" at the candidate show | Louis Dalrymple., 1866-1905, artist | N.Y. : Published by Keppler & Schwarzmann, 1895 November 20. Crossing The Street Saturday morning found me in the standard conditions of the American political writer: under-caffeinated, over-curious, and operating on substantially less sleep than any responsible human should allow himself to function on. Sleep was no longer a partner; sleep was a creditor. I finished the farm chores, grabbed the camera, and headed for Castor HQ, with one stop at the local coffee house for a cup of black brew strong enough to restart whatever was left of the nervous system. Weeks earlier I'd taken the temperature of my own party, from parking lots, sidewalks, and half-empty halls across Republican America. The rebel waves. The factions sniffing at the vacuum that opens the day Trump's term ends. That was the easy gig. This morning, I was crossing the street. During my own run for Congress, I'd gotten to know Neil Manimala, a Democratic candidate for Hillsborough County Commission, a decent man knocking doors in the heat for an office most people can't name. I asked to tag along one Saturday, to look the Democrat voter in the eye outside the ballrooms and the press conferences. He invited me to a joint door-knocking event with Congressman Kathy Castor. Kathy Castor. The champion with the belt. A powerhouse for over a decade, now in the fight of her life, not because of the challenger, but because of the arena. Somebody redrew the map and moved the ring while she was still standing in it. Home-field advantage, gone. I'd watched her from the nosebleeds. I'd reviewed the tape. I'd imagined the debate stage over and over again. And now here she was, ten feet away, working the room like a woman who had personally requested every one of these people's Saturday mornings. Hugs and handshakes freely going around. This was no laptop campaign run out of a basement to a mailing list. This was the ancient and thoroughly undignified business of asking human beings for help with your face. I was impressed, and I hated being impressed. The room held maybe thirty people, every age, every color. Signs on every flat surface, signs stacked against the walls, signs leaning on signs like drunks propping up drunks. No chairs. Thirty volunteers and not one chair. A set designer had built a movie set of a campaign and forgotten the furniture. A real campaign headquarters. And a movie set. Both. That's the whole country in one room, if you squint. Since the threshold, a low electric dread had been building in my sternum. Not a country-club Republican who writes a check and goes home, the actual guy who'd tried to take her belt. Would they smell it on me? Would some sharp-eyed volunteer with a clipboard call me out in front of thirty strangers? Or worse, would they just assume I was one of them and start telling me secrets I wasn't supposed to hear? Kathy made her rounds, shaking hands, thanking people, making each of them feel like the most important person in Hillsborough County. When she got to me, she put out her hand. "Thank you for coming, it's good to see you." "Kathy, it's good to finally meet you. I'm Gavriel." Something flickered behind her eyes, perhaps recognition, perhaps a recollection she couldn't quite pin down. Then she moved along to the man on my left. Which meant she knew, or she didn't, and I couldn't tell, and not knowing wasn't any better. Then Castor called the room to silence. She talked about the week's goal, veterans, about respect for the military, about the work she'd keep doing in Congress. "Why don't we all introduce ourselves--" And here it came again, the question I'd been carrying since the parking lot. Announce I'm here for The American Kitchen Table, writing about the state of their party, and lose the chance to see, unadulterated, what drags a person off the couch to knock on strangers' doors? "--and if you have a rank or a title, introduce yourself with that." She handed me a clean out. Thank G-d. The veterans went first. A man stood and introduced himself as the first Black general in Special Forces, General Remo Butler. Two others who were retired colonels, one of them West Point. Then my turn. I stood up and said the truth, albeit not the whole truth. "I'm PFC Soriano, invited by Neil. I served in the US Army; the military is my family's legacy. My wife served too. First the Army, then the Navy. So, as you can imagine, it got interesting around the house during the Army-Navy games. Go Army!" Everyone laughed. I thought, Beautiful, I've survived. I could go back to being furniture, a quiet man near the signs, watching the machine work. Good Morning, America Retired Gen. Remo took charge the way I imagine he took charge of everything for thirty years, and nobody in the room was dumb enough to tell him no, so he set the room himself. He started praising Kathy's work for veterans, then he told us all we needed to come together and carry her across the finish line. It was a moving speech. I sat there wondering how many versions of that speech he'd given in his life, in how many rooms, to how many men who needed to hear it. Then he called it. "Let's get a photo. All of us vets." I pressed myself deeper into the wall. The old trick. The one you learn when you'd rather be furniture, the one that works right up until it doesn't. Today it didn't. My age and my face and whatever else they saw in me made sure I stuck out like a thumb. Neil and I traded a look. I couldn't read his. I don't know what mine said, but I'd bet it said please, G-d, not today. I mumbled something about humbly declining. They insisted. And here's the thing, you don't deny fellow men in arms a photo. Doesn't matter what banner you fly, what ballot you pull, who you voted for last time. You both put on that uniform. That's a debt that doesn't care about party. I reluctantly unpeeled myself from the wall and got in the frame. A general. Two colonels. A PFC who'd spent the last ten minutes trying to merge through drywall. The commotion of everybody fighting for a spot in the frame. One of the colonels, a small bent-over old man, kept shuffling around hunting for an angle he liked, like a man trying to find the good side of a bad hand. I was second from the General. Shoulder to shoulder. Photo face on. Then he started talking. Everyone stared at us. And that's when it landed on me like an almighty clean right hand from Iron Mike that knocked out Michael Spinks in 91 seconds: this was not a photo. This was an endorsement video. Remo was speaking, live, red dot burning, and I was standing in the shot. "Good morning. I'm Brigadier General, retired, Special Forces, Remo Butler. I am supporting Congresswoman Kathy Castor for reelection because she shows what it's all about. She reaches across the aisle. She knows how to talk to everyone. And she will work very, very hard for us, and she will make this an inclusive party." My head was spinning like I'd slammed five shots of whiskey back-to-back on an empty stomach. The general finished. Then he looked at me. Just a look. And somewhere in the back of my skull a single word detonated: #@! I could see everything happening to me and through me at the same time, like watching my own body get hijacked from the cheap seats. Every exit ran through the same two problems: don't embarrass Neil, and don't be the one** who ruins the momentum the room just built. Two simple rules and a live microphone pointed at my face. I said the only thing that showed up to work that morning. I support her support for veterans. That's what I remember saying. That's what my mouth did while my brain stood off to the side, hands on hips, watching in horror. And the whole time I was cursing myself. Fanatically. A running filibuster of self-loathing in the privacy of my own skull while my face delivered calm, measured, veteran-adjacent words into a rolling camera. Here's the funny thing, I've answered hostile questions at candidate forums. I've learned how explosives work as a combat engineer, how to read a fuse, how to time a charge, how to stay calm when the thing in your hands wants to kill you. All of that. All of that was easier than this. Standing shoulder to shoulder with a general and a live red dot, being asked to choose a tribe in real time. A bomb you can study. A camera eats you alive. The rest followed. More words. I don't fully remember which ones. And when it was over, I was flooded with this pathetic, enormous relief, not because I'd said the right thing, but because it was done. The line had moved. The room had moved on. For one shining second, I was free. I knew I'd have to deal with this later. But right now? I was just a writer again. Camera around my neck. Nobody looking at me. For now. We combat engineers have an unofficial saying. It's our problem until it isn't anymore. Meaning, while you're working the charge, the thing is yours to handle. The second it stops being your problem, it's because you're dead. So, either way, problem solved. Very comforting. Standing in that frame, live red dot, a general's words rolling through me, and every exit closing at once, I remembered the saying. It was my problem. Unfortunately, I was still alive, which meant I had to keep dealing with it. The Ground Game The parking lot was empty. Thirty people had filled that war room thirty-five minutes ago and now gone. Vanished. Like they'd been rented for the hour and returned when the shoot wrapped. I stood in the lot wondering if any of them had actually lived here or if they all materialized for the camera and dissolved back into whatever furniture they came from. I rode with Josh. Neil's campaign manager. A kid, early twenties, tall, slim, looking exactly like the generation that's supposed to be too busy playing video games at two in the morning to care about anything. Except he did care. He wanted in. Wanted to be part of the change. Same kids the pundits write off, except this one was driving me around Tampa with a clipboard and a plan. We took off. And then he showed me the app. This is where I started feeling stupid. You type in the zone numbers, the addresses pop up on a map, you tap one, and it hands you everything: the script, the talking points, instructions for what to do when the door opens and what to do when nobody answers. Door-to-door canvassing, fully automated. Push-button politics. A whole voter file turned into a game you could play with your thumb. It took me straight back to the days I worked at FedEx. Same system. Same maps, same little address pins, same beeping little machine telling a grown man where to go and what to say when he got there. I'd spent years working that kind of route without ever once thinking of it as political strategy. And then it hit me, sitting in a kid's car, watching him drive with one hand and point at a screen with the other. I had run my own congressional campaign barebones. Bare knuckles. No app. No map. No script. Just me, a clipboard, and whatever charm I could scrape together at a stranger's door. Meanwhile the other side had a generation of Josh's running the block like a video game. The kid wasn't the future of the party. The kid was the party. And I'd been running against it with a pencil. Once Josh and I left Castor HQ, we got to talking in the car. I was asking him questions, trying to understand what makes a kid his age sign up for this. He told me he'd always cared about politics, that his generation cared too, they just didn't show up. He was one of the ones who did. I asked him whether he'd noticed a rebel faction in his own party, people who wanted to vote against anything with the word establishment stamped on it. When I said the word, he paused. As if he didn't understand the word in this context. Then he answered. "Yeah, there was a group. A faction that hated corporate candidates. Politicians tied to the corporate machine." And that's when I started noticing it. Every time I said establishment, he said corporate. Same frustration. Same enemy. Different word. It's the difference between Spanish dialects. A Puerto Rican and a Chilean both speak Spanish but say guagua to one and you're talking about a bus, say it to the other and you're talking about a baby. Same language. Different map. And you can stand there shouting bus, bus, bus at the downtown express and a man turns around frantically looking for a baby. American politics. Same frustration, different dialect. We got to the doors. I looked at the itinerary. Castor had told the room herself: non-MAGA Republicans, independents, disillusioned Democrats, Libertarians. Not the base. The middle. Smart, if you're trying to win. The doors themselves were the real education. I knocked twelve. Spoke to four. What surprised me wasn't what these people believed. It was how little they'd thought about it at all. I asked what issues were hurting them. They'd shrug. Cost of living? Yeah. Insurance? Yeah, that too. They agreed with whatever I suggested and offered almost nothing of their own. Not disengaged exactly. Just elsewhere. Living their lives while politics happened around them like weather. But one voter stuck out to me. An African American man, mid-thirties, in his garage behind a screen. He was busy cleaning pieces of a machine he'd taken apart, laid out neat on a cloth like a surgeon's tray. The garage was spotless. Couch against the wall. Sports paraphernalia nailed up like trophies. A TV, a cooler, a shelf of odds and ends. A proper man cave. A place a man goes to feel small on purpose, to get away from the world and its troubles and just be nobody for a while. The kind of man who cared about his country and his community, you could feel it coming off him without him saying a word about it. And yet. Uninspired. By everyone. I gave him the spiel. He told me the Republicans had already come by. "Yeah, they came before. Honestly, I don't know who I'm voting for. I don't even know if I'm going to vote." "You've got a lot going on," I said. "Last thing you've got time for is sifting through candidates and the bs." He chuckled. "For sure. I don't know. I really don't know. I know I have to vote, but I don't know." I asked what he wanted elected officials to fix. "Honestly? I don't know." "Cost of living?" He shrugged. "Yeah, things are more expensive." He never got up from the chair. Never stopped cleaning the machine. Thanked me and admitted he hadn't looked into the election, said it like a confession, like he was letting me down, like the whole thing was one more chore on a list already too long. I've sold things for a living, and I know the sound of a door that's still open. He wasn't gone. He wasn't a lost vote. He was a man sitting on the line of certainty, waiting for the right person to make him believe again. Somebody had to show up and give him a reason. Nobody had. Not us Republicans. And not the Democrats. We parted on good terms. He stayed in the chair. The machine stayed in pieces. He wasn't excited about anyone. Neither was anyone else I talked to. The campaigns come. They knock. They deliver. They leave. But does anyone believe? The Man & The Machine After my doors I met up with Josh. He gave me one more address, then we'd be done. On our walk back to the car he told me about a Venezuelan woman he'd been speaking with in Spanish, complaining about Trump and Venezuela, and I wondered how much he understood. "That's odd, most Venezuelans I speak with are happy about what's going on." We finally got back to the car and drove off. I kept asking questions. This time about David Jolly. "Well, there's a reason I'm not out knocking doors for Jolly. I come from a circle of progressive liberals, my friends and I, and Jolly isn't progressive enough. Too much of a reach across." Then the punchline. "But I'll vote for him." And there it was. The exact same contradiction I'd spent the whole year writing about on my side of the aisle. Voters who hate the establishment, who say the party abandoned them, who won't lift a finger for the candidate, and who show up anyway and pull the lever with their name on it. I'd written about this among anti-establishment Republicans. Now a progressive Democrat was handing me the same disease. I was frank with him: "Purely looking at this with the eye of a strategist, Jolly's exactly what you need. You want to win Florida? You need somebody who reaches past the base. Independents. Disillusioned Republicans. The middle. You can't win the governorship by campaigning to the people who already agree with you." Then we got to the presidential race. Was there anybody progressives wanted? He didn't have an answer. "Well, no, not really. Kamala. None of us want Kamala. That's ridiculous. Newsom. We don't want Newsom either. He's corporate. He's such a corporate machine." Corporate. Again. The word had been tailing us all day like a puppy dog. Yet when I asked who he felt in his heart should be the nominee? Nothing. He knew who he hated. He didn't know who he loved. He knew the type of politician he was against. Couldn't name the one he was for. Sound familiar? I'd heard Republicans say almost the exact same thing about their own leadership. And I didn't leave convinced Josh would sit out a Harris or Newsom nomination, either. He'd vote Jolly despite hating him. That's the tell. Republicans complain about the establishment. Democrats complain about the corporate machine. Republicans say the party sold out its voters to the establishment. Democrats say it sold out to corporations. Both have a base that feels ignored. Both have a faction that thinks the party betrayed its soul. Both vote the nominee anyway in November. That doesn't make the parties the same. Different philosophies. Different policies. Different country, maybe. But the feeling? The feeling was the same feeling in a different suit. By the end of the drive, it had all come together, and the thing that tied it shut was that one word. Corporate. That was Josh's word for establishment. Two rooms, two dialects, one broken machine, and everybody yelling bus, bus, bus at a man who only hears baby. Republicans scream establishment. Democrats scream corporate. Both mean the same thing: the guys with the money and the microphone rigged it, and nobody's coming to fix your street. Same disease, two dialects, and both sides convinced the other room is full of devils who wouldn't understand a word of it. I stood in both rooms this year. I watched a loyalist beg eight people to hold a line that had already snapped. I watched a progressive kid who'd hate the governor he was going to vote for anyway. And in between, in a spotless garage, I watched a good man sit still in a chair, cleaning a machine that was already in pieces, because nobody had given him one single reason to believe. The campaigns will knock again. They'll hand out the same script in a different accent and call it a movement. And the man in the garage will still be sitting there, machine in pieces, waiting for somebody to give him a reason. -- Gavriel Soriano Every One A King Your voice strengthens our collective power. name: Dan Schwartz
subject: Harris threatened to arrest WHO?!
body:
A reporter asked Andy Harris about the Iran war. He threatened to have her arrested.
After my debate Tuesday night, a reporter asked my opponent, Congressman Andy Harris, the chair of the House Freedom Caucus, about his support for Trump’s war in Iran... and he had a full-blown meltdown.
He told her she was breaking the law by recording him, which she wasn’t, and threatened to have the police remove her.
[](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261014-3.l4h_Ij&refcode=em20261014-2112&%3Bamount=5&t=1&akid=2112%2E1086043%2E8I40mO)
If we haven’t met yet, I’m Dan Schwartz, and I’m running for Congress in Maryland’s First District. I’m a parent and a consumer watchdog, and I’ve spent my career holding banks and corporations accountable for regular people. Wes Moore told me I could reach out to you because we’re both in this fight to hold the far right accountable and flip the House for Democrats.
I understand why that question rattled him. Earlier that night, on stage, he blamed Democrats' environmental rules for the spike in diesel prices, and the room laughed at him. Everyone in MD-01 knows exactly when those prices took off. It was when Trump started a war with Iran, and Congressman Andy Harris backed it.
**[DONATE NOW››](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261014-3.l4h_Ij&amount=5&refcode=em-20261014-3&t=2&akid=2112%2E1086043%2E8I40mO)**
Diesel runs MD-01. It's in the farmer's tractor, the waterman's boat, and the truck that stocks the grocery store, and all of them have been paying more since the war started. Harris would rather blame Democrats than say one word against the president who started it, and when someone asks him to, he calls for the police.
This is the same congressman who hasn't held an in-person town hall since 2023. He doesn't like questions from voters, and on Tuesday he made it clear he doesn't like them from reporters either.
**Our latest poll has us down just 1 point. Beating Harris takes the Freedom Caucus chair out of Congress and flips a seat that helps Democrats take back the House.**
**[If you can, split a $25 donation with me and Wes Moore to support the Democratic ticket and help keep our ads running across the district through Election Day.](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261014-3.l4h_Ij&refcode=em-20261014-3&t=3&akid=2112%2E1086043%2E8I40mO)**
**[Donate $25 ››](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/1438?c0=wes-em-20261014-3.jKnGsq&refcode=em-20261014-3&t=22&akid=2112%2E1086043%2E8I40mO)**
Thanks,
Dan Schwartz
[](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261014-3.l4h_Ij&refcode=em20261014-2112&%3Bamount=5&t=23&akid=2112%2E1086043%2E8I40mO)

| | The last time a Democrat won a Senate seat in Kansas was **1932.** But that nearly century-long political drought could be on the verge of ending. **Republicans are now rushing millions of dollars into Kansas to bail out incumbent Roger Marshall — because they're spooked by recent polling and a series of horrible headlines.** [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/141436191/653545495/-2111990565?refcode=2026-10-14-ks&recurring=&amount=3&amounts=10,30,50,100,200&refcode2=d59cae31-2dc8-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDEvMS84OTQxMiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkNTljYWUzMS0yZGM4LWYxMTEtYmY1Yi0wMDBkM2E0ZmJlODMiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=tGRWTmkiAmKtUuPp_y9RF1cd4z582WxGCxxCBHu5NbY=) Marshall's campaign has been rocked by the revelation that, **as a doctor, he sued hundreds of patients for outstanding medical bills**(often tiny sums). body:
I haven't forgotten where I came from, and I never will. | _Interested in these updates? Click any of the links below to let us know you still want to hear from Wesley and our team._
---

Peter,

With **Election Day just 20 days out,** I wanted to take a moment to reintroduce myself, share a little about where I come from, and explain why I decided to run for Congress in the first place.

I was born and raised in North St. Louis County, in a union household where I learned the value of hard work, service, and looking out for the people around you. My father was a police officer, and my mother worked for the federal government.

Growing up, I saw firsthand how hard-working families had to fight to get ahead. And I learned early on that when people come together and stand up for one another, they can make a real difference. **Those lessons have stayed with me my entire life.**

They've guided me through law school, my work as a public defender, and my time serving as St. Louis County Prosecuting Attorney, where I worked to make our justice system fairer and more accountable. Those same values led me to run for Congress. Because I believe the people of Missouri deserve someone who understands the challenges they're facing. Someone who will fight to lower costs, protect their rights, and make sure working families have a fair shot at getting ahead.

That's what I came to Washington to do. And it's work I'm determined to continue. But with November 3rd approaching, we have a lot riding on this election. We have an opportunity to take back our Democratic House majority, hold this administration accountable, and get Congress back to working for the people it's supposed to serve. **And right now, we're coming up on an important mid-month fundraising deadline.**

I'm asking for your support because everything we raise between now and Election Day helps us keep reaching voters, building our grassroots movement, and fighting for the future our communities deserve. [**Can I count on you to chip in $5, or whatever you can, before our mid-month fundraising deadline to ensure we don't fall behind?**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/141436257/653549663/114933067?refcode=em26_261014_mm1_fndd_gq_act___WB_ettx&utm_campaign=em26_261014_mm1_fndd_gq_act___WB_ettx&utm_medium=email&refcode2=ac962420-2ec8-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNTkvMS8xMDYzODkiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYWM5NjI0MjAtMmVjOC1mMTExLWJmNWItMDAwZDNhNGZiZTgzIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=WxxlL2CeeYZ1_gETTuNGJfs-WtyF0M3aqp16f-YsYl0=)

Peter, With Election Day just 20 days out, I wanted to take a moment to reintroduce myself, share a little about where I come from, and explain why I decided to run for Congress in the first place. I was born and raised in North St. Louis County, in a union household where I learned the value of hard work, service, and looking out for the people around you. My father was a police officer, and my mother worked for the federal government. Growing up, I saw firsthand how hard-working families had to fight to get ahead. And I learned early on that when people come together and stand up for one another, they can make a real difference. Those lessons have stayed with me my entire life. They've guided me through law school, my work as a public defender, and my time serving as St. Louis County Prosecuting Attorney, where I worked to make our justice system fairer and more accountable. Those same values led me to run for Congress. Because I believe the people of Missouri deserve someone who understands the challenges they're facing. Someone who will fight to lower costs, protect their rights, and make sure working families have a fair shot at getting ahead. That's what I came to Washington to do. And it's work I'm determined to continue. But with November 3rd approaching, we have a lot riding on this election. We have an opportunity to take back our Democratic House majority, hold this administration accountable, and get Congress back to working for the people it's supposed to serve. Then-Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody looks on as Governor Ron DeSantis speaks at a press conference at the Lakeland, Florida Police Department in 2021. Photo by Paul Hennessy/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images.
During her tenure as Florida Attorney General, Sen. Ashley Moody led an investigation into the work-release program that allowed Jeffrey Epstein to engage in sexual encounters while imprisoned for soliciting underage girls for prostitution. After nearly two years of probing, she concluded no wrongdoing. Now Moody, a Republican, is up for reelection in a tight race for a Florida Senate seat against Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon, and she has received $50,000 from individuals connected to Epstein.
Douglas Band, a former Bill Clinton staffer who communicated with Ghislaine Maxwell to schedule meetings between the former president and Jeffrey Epstein, donated $14,000 to Moody's victory fund on April 15. Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman and John Catsimatidis, two billionaires who appeared respectively in call logs and address books in the Epstein files, donated the next most to Moody's fund at $12,000 and $10,000 a pop. Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan, another billionaire who maintained a relationship with Epstein even after the disgraced financier had been jailed for solicitation of prostitution from a minor, and Ronald Lauder, the billionaire heir to the Estee Lauder companies who appeared in the Epstein files for meetings and joint purchasing agreements with Epstein, both chipped in $7,000.
Moody announced her probe on August 6, 2019, four days before Epstein's death and shortly after Gov. Ron DeSantis ordered the transfer of an internal investigation being conducted by Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw to the Florida Department Of Law Enforcement. Two days later on August 8, Moody immediately found that the work release had not been authorized by a judge. ("We have not been able to locate any administrative order, nothing in the transcript, that would indicate that the judge was aware of ordered work release in this particular case," she told local media.) Yet it took almost two years for her office to finish investigating how law enforcement allowed Epstein's work release to go forward.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZHJvcHNpdGVuZXdzLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.3HMPP2Q9Chvav8E871DeUE8j5bKu6tui1QuMChMQTQ4?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=220430953)
NBC News has [since substantiated claims](https://substack.com/redirect/11f3f8af-e7aa-4aef-9aa1-ed76eaa8d222?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that Epstein abused the Palm Beach work-release program, which allowed eligible inmates to leave detention for up to 16 hours a day, multiple days a week, to resume working their jobs or completing approved projects. They reported in June 2026 that, "At least five women say they had sexual encounters with Epstein while he was participating in the jail's now-defunct work-release program, according to records released this year by the Justice Department as part of the agency's Epstein investigation. The encounters occurred at his office in West Palm Beach and in a car parked outside the county jail, the women said in FBI interviews."
Nevertheless, Moody's FDLE investigation wrapped up in May 2021, concluding no noticeable misconduct by the sheriff's office or state prosecutors in Palm Beach County in granting Epstein said work release. Upon the conclusion of the investigation, former FBI agent Stuart Kaplan criticized its lack of search warrants, subpoenas, or a grand jury. "It appears the FDLE solely depended upon the cooperation and memory of those involved," Kaplan [told West Palm Beach TV](https://substack.com/redirect/e89b1182-de62-46ef-b87a-6a6cc74a26d3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Sarah Kellen, a former aide to Epstein, testified before the House Oversight Committee that Epstein paid Palm Beach County law enforcement officers for preferential treatment, though she did not specify how much.
Ashley Moody's campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Florida's U.S. Senate race has only recently come into play electorally as President Donald Trump's abysmal approval ratings have dragged downballot GOP candidates underwater across the country. Amid his unpopular war in Iran, the president has seen his favorability in the sunshine state [shift from](https://substack.com/redirect/7d926aa3-46c4-486b-aa60-4c7d83217876?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) +9 at the start of his second term to -14 with three weeks until election day, according to Civiqs.
Meanwhile, Nixon, an insurgent now endorsed by Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, overcame a roughly 17:1 fundraising disadvantage in the Democratic primary to upset the establishment's pick, Alex Vindman, on August 18. Since then, [polls have shown](https://substack.com/redirect/3c52c790-4438-42a1-ae72-945ee75e4097?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Nixon closing within as few as 2 percentage points of Moody.
Sanders recently announced four joint Fighting Oligarchy campaign events set to take place with Nixon on October 17 and 18 in Tampa, Melbourne, Gainesville, and Tallahassee. An ascendant national figure, Nixon has campaigned on a bold progressive agenda that includes Medicare for All, a federal jobs guarantee with inflation adjusted wages, universal childcare, and a national rent freeze and moratorium on evictions.
Moody, on the other hand, cast the deciding vote in July 2025 to table an NDAA amendment that would have directed the Attorney General to "make publicly available documents related to Jeffrey Epstein," and has at every turn defended the Trump administration's illegal war in Iran, voting 12 times against War Powers Resolutions.
Fast forward one year to July 2026, Moody positioned herself as a key defender of Attorney General Todd Blanche, a key architect of the Epstein files coverup, during his confirmation hearing to succeed Pam Bondi at the DOJ. While Democrats highlighted his role in burying the files and past as Trump's personal attorney, Moody listed awards Blanche received while he "prosecuted drug traffickers and violent criminals" as a prosecutor in the Southern District of New York.
Trump has returned the favor for her loyalty, [offering](https://substack.com/redirect/0092d460-a97a-4527-b347-bea35194c6ee?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Moody his "Complete and Total Endorsement" and saying the passage of the Big Beautiful Bill "probably wouldn't have happened" without her. Moody [accepted Trump's endorsement](https://substack.com/redirect/4bd6efe1-1488-45cf-a44b-e361e37121a1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in stride, saying she's "incredibly honored" to have his support.

Yet it took almost two years for her office to finish investigating how law enforcement allowed Epstein's work release to go forward. NBC News has that Epstein abused the Palm Beach work-release program, which allowed eligible inmates to leave detention for up to 16 hours a day, multiple days a week, to resume working their jobs or completing approved projects. The encounters occurred at his office in West Palm Beach and in a car parked outside the county jail, the women said in FBI interviews." Nevertheless, Moody's FDLE investigation wrapped up in May 2021, concluding no noticeable misconduct by the sheriff's office or state prosecutors in Palm Beach County in granting Epstein said work release. Upon the conclusion of the investigation, former FBI agent Stuart Kaplan criticized its lack of search warrants, subpoenas, or a grand jury. "It appears the FDLE solely depended upon the cooperation and memory of those involved," Kaplan . Sarah Kellen, a former aide to Epstein, testified before the House Oversight Committee that Epstein paid Palm Beach County law enforcement officers for preferential treatment, though she did not specify how much. | | Dear Friend,
For months, I have been calling for bold action to lower costs, cut government red tape, protect Maryland communities, and make our state more affordable. Now, with Election Day approaching just weeks away, Governor Wes Moore has announced executive actions addressing several of those same issues. He is in a desperate launch to save his failings as Governor and ever-falling approval rating. _**Take a look at this timeline:**_ **Data Centers:** Dan has been calling for a moratorium on data center development from the beginning of his campaign.
* **September 23:** Governor Moore issued an executive order establishing a statewide review framework and task force.

**Permitting and Housing: **Dan has advocated reducing burdensome regulations and accelerating permitting from the very start.
* **October 1: **Governor Moore issued executive orders addressing permitting delays and housing innovation.

**Fuel Costs:** Dan has already called for suspending Maryland's gas tax as a key aspect to his platform.
* **October 9:** Governor Moore issued an emergency order providing targeted diesel fuel relief for farmers and forestry operators.

**Tolls and Fees:** Dan has consistently advocated cutting taxes, tolls, and fees since Day 1 of his campaign, and in his personal advocacy apart from campaigning.
* **October 14:** Governor Moore announced a one-year toll pause.

_**Wes Moore is changing his tune, but only to try and buy your vote. He's lied before and he's doing it again.**_
Friend, with **November 3rd just 20 days away**, it is more important than ever for me to continue to combat the dishonestly of Wes Moore. He can try to use these bandaids to get him through Election Day, but the very moment he were to get re-elected, he would not only continue the destruction he has caused our state--**he would make it even more grave.** That's why I need you. Please join my team tonight and help me continue to run a good, hard race against Wes Moore all the way to the finish line. We are up on TV, are sending out targeted mailings and text campaigns, and so much more. I am working very hard for you.

I know Wes Moore has made finances difficult in our state, but [will you consider contributing any amount to help me tonight?](https://us.list-manage.com/nDYIQuJee_G?e=5bb5efcda7&c2id=56a77d5a7be3731f6f21d9e4cc6a323b) Every dollar will go directly to flipping crucial votes. And we can do this! We are already seeing the profit of these contributions in the Blue Corridor with many swing Democrats and Independents agreeing with my platform and begging for us to win to bring real relief.

Thank you for being a part of this movement and supporting me. Let's win!

For Maryland,

Dan Cox
Nominee for Governor of Maryland

Hi Peter,
I talk a lot about the state of our country as an OB-GYN and as a member of Congress. But today, I want to talk about it as a mom, because I’d be lying if I said I’m not worried about my kids’ futures. The world feels heavy right now. Healthcare is a mess. Access to reproductive care is under constant attack – birth control, abortion access, all of it. One in three counties in America has no OB-GYN and nowhere to give birth. Republicans made the single largest cut to healthcare in our nation’s history, despite repeated warnings that it would drive up costs. They chose tax breaks for billionaires anyway, and now Minnesotans are facing a double-digit increase in their insurance costs. And it goes beyond healthcare. The surging violence we are seeing – against women, immigrants, people of color – is horrifying. The Pentagon is planning to livestream an execution, and our president called for a foreign nation to bomb two American cities during a campaign speech. This is horrifying and cannot become our new norm. As a parent, I’m deeply troubled by what our nation is becoming. We’re hardening as a society in ways that scare me. But I refuse to lose sight of what we are fighting for – because that’s exactly what this administration is counting on. A safer, more affordable, more just America is possible. Access to quality healthcare and an economy that works for all of us, not just the wealthiest, is possible. An immigration system grounded in safety, dignity, and justice is possible. Leaders who put people over profits are possible. The fact is that elections matter – and now more than ever before we need to elect leaders who share in the same vision of America, and who want to make this country better for our kids. We can do it all, but it all comes down to these final days. Tonight at 11:59 PM ET (8:59 PM PT) is our final FEC deadline before Election Day. The report that follows is the last public look at our campaign’s strength before voters cast their ballots.

David Valadao and his Republican allies have committed $14.3 million to buy this seat, and the best response possible would be to show huge grassroots support for our campaign.

body:

It’s
Jocelyn Benson.

We’re coming up on our last reporting deadline, and I could use your help.
[ https://act.jocelynbenson.com/go/21969?amount=25&t=1002&akid=1997%2E181023%2EMLE-Gy ]Will you step up today
and make your first contribution to our campaign before our last reporting
deadline?

[ https://act.jocelynbenson.com/go/21969?t=1003&akid=1997%2E181023%2EMLE-Gy ]Donate →

I’m in this race because I believe everyone deserves a fair shot in life.
It’s why I started my career in Alabama working on civil rights, then as a
law clerk to a federal civil rights judge in Detroit, and now, as
Secretary of State of Michigan, where I fight every day to protect and
expand voting rights.

And it’s why I’m committed to building this campaign for governor from the
ground up, from thousands of individual contributors – not billionaires or
corporate PACs.

While my Republican counterpart has already accepted $6 million from the
DeVos family funneled into a shady super PAC, I am running to represent
YOU. I won’t be beholden to any corporation or billionaire donor.

But, I
can’t do it alone. After Trump won Michigan in 2024, all eyes are on this
race to see if we can keep the governor’s office blue in November.

The latest polls show what we’ve known for a while: this race is going to
be extremely close. We can’t take any deadline or vote for granted.

FINAL FILING DEADLINE: **OCTOBER 15th**

| | | | | | | | | | | |

Peter,
It's that time again, and this time, _it's the last one._
At the end of every three months, campaigns across the country submit their fundraising totals to the Federal Election Commission (FEC). But these Quarterly Reports do a lot more than tell the FEC who donated.
_They're a campaign's report card._
They show the media, House leadership, and my opponent how healthy and competitive our campaign really is. **And Peter this is our FINAL filing deadline report before Election Day.** There are no more chances after this. The final countdown has begun.
That's why we've set our most important goal yet: $25,000 before midnight on October 15th.
**HELP US HIT $25,000 BEFORE THE FILING DEADLINE →**
A strong report tells everyone watching that Central New York is ready for change, and that this seat is ready to FLIP. A weak one tells the Democrat Machine they can coast to November.
_I grew up in Auburn in a blue-collar family. I know what it means to work hard, do everything right, and still wonder why it keeps getting harder to get ahead. I'm running to lower costs, back law enforcement, protect our family farms, and give President Trump another reliable America First vote in the House._
But none of that happens unless we finish this race strong.
[**Will you chip in $26, $50, $100, or whatever you can to help us earn an A+ on our filing report card?**](https://us.list-manage.com/kZ634ISeP7s?e=7e42b80a6c&c2id=65ca27defa2b2ff4fbda44443b52d843)

[Let's show them exactly how strong we are.](https://us.list-manage.com/kMkbveu8WGX?e=7e42b80a6c&c2id=65ca27defa2b2ff4fbda44443b52d843)

→ Wisconsin would be led by **one of the MOST conservative Wisconsin House members in modern history**. He supports dangerous abortion bans and restrictions on reproductive healthcare.
→ Our state will be at the whim of Donald Trump and his millionaire friends – **not Wisconsin families.**

Friends, Tonight at midnight is the last FEC fundraising deadline of the 2026 election — our _final_ chance before Election Day to show Democrats’ strength. Over the past few months, so many of you have stepped up when I’ve asked, and I’m profoundly grateful for that. You’ve donated, volunteered, made calls, come to events, and shared these emails with friends and family. And now that voting has begun in California, I love hearing from so many of you that you’ve already cast your ballot — that’s my favorite thing to see in my inbox, so thank you for sharing! **If we flip the House in three weeks, and I believe we can and we will, it will be because of people like YOU staying engaged all the way to the finish line.** I’m energized for what comes next. Ballots go out Friday. Tonight is our last FEC deadline before Election Day.

---
| | Good evening,

Ballots land in mailboxes across Washington on Friday and every day after that is Election Day.

Before voting officially begins, let’s talk about where things stand.

Trump’s war, his tariffs, and his corruption are hurting families here at home. Even the most extreme Republicans are starting to realize they could be in trouble this election.

**But we can’t wait until Election Day to get things done - not when _millions of Americans are being kicked off their health care and struggling to afford gas and groceries._**

In the last few weeks, I have taken action by:
* Introducing bipartisan legislation on intergenerational housing
* Voting to move forward Rep. Al Green’s motion to impeach Trump
* Standing up for Head Start, which this administration keeps trying to dismantle
* Going on national television (CNN) to make sure Americans know exactly what this president is doing to them

**And most importantly, I kept showing up at home in WA-10:** meeting the next class of Ordinary Seamen at the Youth Marine Foundation, championing our maritime industry, securing funding for Habitat for Humanity of Tacoma, and stopping by the Apple Squeeze in Steilacoom.

**Because this is the job you elected me to do. I fight in DC and I deliver for the South Sound - and there’s no one who can do it better.**

**Now, in 20 days we have a real chance to hold extremist Republicans and Trump accountable but to do that we need to get over the final hurdle and take back the House.**

**_Tonight at midnight is our last FEC deadline before Election Day._** The numbers we post tonight are the final reports used by strategists to determine who’s vulnerable. We need them to know WA-10 isn’t available to them.

[Will you chip in before midnight to show we’re ready to work and we’re going to finish strong?](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/141437937/653586062/-487694537?amount=25&refcode=MS_EM_FR_90DO_261014_1_1&refcode2=cf57cb25-46c8-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS83OTQ0OSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjZjU3Y2IyNS00NmM4LWYxMTEtYmY1Yi0wMDBkM2E0ZmJlODMiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=8uF2SnTVrWOqrBUCW3azr4KaOvnlQrOi7mCqMiGry4g=)

body:

---
_You're getting this message because you’ve supported good causes and Democratic candidates. We need your support to continue fighting for our democracy. We love having you in our network, but if you only want our most important email updates,[click here.](https://act.blueampaction.com/go/108?t=2&akid=3513%2E259176%2EeF35ep) If you'd like to unsubscribe, [click here.](https://act.blueampaction.com/go/109?t=3&akid=3513%2E259176%2EeF35ep)_

[](https://act.blueampaction.com/go/18655?source=SL_EM_FR_2026.10.15_Crow-Intimidate_B1_F1_S2_C1_180AC-360DON_T2&t=4&akid=3513%2E259176%2EeF35ep) Trump can threaten me, but he'll never intimidate me.

I'm Jason Crow, Paratrooper, Army Ranger, and Democratic Congressman from Colorado. I served three combat tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and earned a Bronze Star for my service, so when a 5-time draft dodger calls _me_ a traitor, you'll forgive me for not shaking in my boots.

**To lead in this moment requires us to be bold and unafraid._Trump is neither._**

He and his cronies — like Pete Hegseth and RFK Jr. — like to play strong men, but they treat their power like a shield they can hide behind. They like to flex, not serve.

Trump doesn't care about you. He's focusing on lining his own pockets, building monuments to himself, and suppressing the vote, because he knows he can't stay in power otherwise. His cabinet is willing to continue letting him play king like this if it means they can have a little power too.

This administration is literally stealing from the poor to give to the rich, cutting Medicaid and food assistance to create new tax breaks for the 1%. They're not "brave" for sending other people's kids to die in wars of choice.

_And they wonder why people are pissed off..._

**Patriot, it’s John James. **
We're less than 3 weeks away from Election Day. Before I say anything else—as someone who has logged 750 combat hours in Iraq—I know every second counts, and there’s not a moment in the day we should be wasting. _I promise I will not waste your time._
I just want to tell you a little about myself; it’s about time we got well-acquainted.
I was born and raised in Michigan, and throughout high school, I felt a deep-rooted call to service. I decided I wouldn’t just read about service in the magazines, _**I would live it.**_
[**Eventually, this led me to apply to West Point, and my decision to serve my country would make me the man I am today.**](https://links.iterable.com/s/c/XHM4eaItmRpe6EooF7ZTZ43eAAx_4aQFxELiGdxwKeWSgKcL8KbcPolH6tenUBuT-R-i_lwJQ7oc4o8-5rXb4xA7xkNRSuYbWzuGQW7gO1sbyFTgrDhLzL0TjJofkJur788YZ4LVRqI4ivWPG7UM9VD6zbt3bFFjC0hkX-D7g70lmAs_F9vpFyDbhegCqI3Ka92-DaZDYBUdqbRult1cCN-WzPs_xdMZjqIJbY78lsDC0Tk1ohjRDx_0W-MwhgxrvsUwze0Byvv2HK-hlNjzgWddSpsS2H-3hojlK8i7RcMVnzG_kw0SopazNRgx583uYpeEoa_Oyiwazt_SbgFtijzvHxIuMCPkYQYhRDOJ6-35u5jqGvqcQFFXBEDkdcfMHFAdyBRc8dMt98vUwUBE9uENW8G2uOwrZFnUUnomr2FE-s86uoENjul319irXbI6cHWydvQnsBLM0b3iZlOYOUHTjYwrv6BICS7SbhTlQexDRqRwFx61UGjZ1BPdysb9n64zuuykeIyKWwq6oVfhJhr7YsWvKUig9ww22dmece5rszeNkHaj9bBb45bzScbHuqROcf40J0VVoqCzI6p-BhYujOcgZDNou3z-VejgG9LhOqfpjA8AGXfvBm6C2g/hXXIhhNDQGvVxqUogkNpQMEIBebXoZYA/25)

Graduating from West Point was just the beginning of my eight years in the United States Army.
During Operation Iraqi Freedom, I led Apache Helicopter Platoons, and I feel like I spent more time in the air than I did on the ground. Some nights, I didn’t know if I’d make it through the next day, and every mission I flew, I went into the unknown. **Throughout my service, I had the honor of receiving a Combat Action Badge and two Air Medals. **

clean_body: My story| | | | | Patriot, it’s John James. We're less than 3 weeks away from Election Day. Before I say anything else—as someone who has logged 750 combat hours in Iraq—I know every second counts, and there’s not a moment in the day we should be wasting. I promise I will not waste your time. I just want to tell you a little about myself; it’s about time we got well-acquainted. I was born and raised in Michigan, and throughout high school, I felt a deep-rooted call to service. I decided I wouldn’t just read about service in the magazines, I would live it. Graduating from West Point was just the beginning of my eight years in the United States Army. During Operation Iraqi Freedom, I led Apache Helicopter Platoons, and I feel like I spent more time in the air than I did on the ground. Some nights, I didn’t know if I’d make it through the next day, and every mission I flew, I went into the unknown. Throughout my service, I had the honor of receiving a Combat Action Badge and two Air Medals. I wouldn’t trade my time in the service for anything, but I’ll be honest, it was good coming home, and I can rest easy knowing I did my country proud. After coming back stateside, I swapped my fatigues for a suit. I took over the family business, creating jobs here in Michigan and earning a master’s in supply chain management from Penn State and an MBA from the University of Michigan. I was never one to rest, and after making so many life-or-death decisions in Iraq, I knew every second mattered; I wanted to make the most of my time for my family and me. I never for a second considered running for office, and the last thing I’d consider myself is a politician... I saw the Democrats destroying our country, and I knew my service to this great nation wasn’t over yet. Everybody told me running for office isn’t easy, but my heart was telling me it was the right thing to do. I won my election, with the help of President Trump, and started delivering results for my new constituents. Then, in 2023, when the Establishment tried to move on from Trump and being MAGA was seen as risky or politically inconvenient, I was among the first in Michigan to endorse President Trump for 2024. Loyalty isn’t a talking point to me; it’s the only way I know how to operate. My dedication to this country, my loyalty towards my constituents, and my desire to see the greatest nation on earth excel are part of the reasons why I’m now emailing you, but they’re not my #1 reason why... These three kids are the reason why I’m sending this message to you, as a TRUMP-ENDORSED Republican and father running to be the next Governor of Michigan. Having my own family taught me more lessons than I could list, and it was the one thing being in the U.S. Army didn’t prepare me for. But it also awoke in me a desire to do EVERYTHING and ANYTHING I can to ensure my kids have bright futures. My family means everything to me, and Michigan is our home; that’s why I will fight like my life depends on it to save this state and win this November. I’m under no illusions; I know this election will be one of the toughest challenges I’ve faced in my entire life, but after everything I’ve done in my service, it’s nothing I can’t handle. Unfortunately, the one thing I can’t directly control is spending, and the Democrats will do everything in their power to stop my campaign from making it to the ballot box this November. Nothing can stop us from saving this country if we stand together. Today, I’m asking you to make a small-dollar gift of $10, $25, $50 or ANYTHING you can spare to fuel my campaign’s fight as we approach our upcoming election for Governor on November 3rd. Thank you for taking the time to read my message. I hope to hear from you in the days to come. name: Ken Burns
subject: We cannot escape history
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Chris Pappas for Senate
body:
We may not be able to outspend them. But we can outsmart them.
[](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20261015_1.DXmBuR&refcode=em20261015-1&t=1&akid=9530%2E582294%2E33Ou8M)
As someone who has spent a lifetime studying our nation’s history, if there is one constant lesson in our past, it’s that our republic is only as strong as the citizens willing to defend it.
And when you spend decades immersed in American history, you begin to see just how much it has to teach us about the moment we are living through today.
Our founders were trying to build a new kind of country – one in which citizens had the responsibility and the privilege to decide for themselves. They understood that Congress had a vital role to play in checking executive power.
_Today we are seeing what happens when that responsibility is abandoned._
Too many leaders have remained silent in the face of corruption, incompetence, tariffs, rising costs, and an executive branch accumulating more and more power.
Chris Pappas has not been silent.
**That is one of the reasons I am so proud to wholeheartedly support Chris for the United States Senate.**
This Senate race is a David and Goliath story.
We know Republicans are going to outspend us. We know millions of dollars from outside interests and billionaires are flowing into New Hampshire.
But they can’t buy the judgment of New Hampshire voters.
Granite Staters are smart enough to distinguish between the interests of billionaires and special interests and the interests of ordinary working people – the people struggling to afford healthcare, those having a hard time at the gas pump, and the small businesses being squeezed by tariffs.
**We may not be able to outspend them. But we can outsmart them.**
**[If you’re able please make a $5 contribution to Chris Pappas today and help him keep fighting for the people of New Hampshire.](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20261015_1.DXmBuR&refcode=em20261015-1&t=2&akid=9530%2E582294%2E33Ou8M)**
**[Donate $5 »](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20261015_1.DXmBuR&amount=5&refcode=em20261015-1&t=21&akid=9530%2E582294%2E33Ou8M)**
The choice before voters is actually quite simple. If you like the way things are going in New Hampshire and across the country – skyrocketing prices and reckless foreign wars – vote Republican. That’s who is in charge.
If you’re ready for change, I urge you to support Chris Pappas.
Just this once I hope we don’t reward silence in the face of corruption and incompetence with our votes.
Because this election is about more than one Senate seat. If Chris wins this open seat, Democrats have a chance to change the Senate and restore some of the checks and balances that are supposed to make our government work.
And that is what we need to be about: repair and restoration.
Abraham Lincoln once wrote, _“We cannot escape history.”_
We cannot escape this moment either. But we can decide what we do with it.
**[So please stand with Chris Pappas and do what you can to help him in these final weeks. This race matters, and Chris needs the resources to compete.](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20261015_1.DXmBuR&refcode=em20261015-1&t=22&akid=9530%2E582294%2E33Ou8M)**
**[Donate $5 »](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20261015_1.DXmBuR&amount=5&refcode=em20261015-1&t=23&akid=9530%2E582294%2E33Ou8M)**
Thank you,
Ken Burns
Granite Stater and Filmmaker
**New Hampshire is poised to be one of the closest Senate races in the country. Will you chip in today to help Chris stop the Republicans from flipping the Granite State red and expanding their Senate majority?**

subject: An important day, Peter!
body:
$500,000 in the next 48 hours. Can we do it?
